content: Classical swine fever (CSF), also known as hog cholera or pig plague (a term derived from the German word Schweinepest), is a highly contagious viral disease that affects domestic pigs and wild boars. The clinical manifestations of CSF include fever, skin lesions, and convulsions. In most cases, particularly in young animals, the disease results in death within 15 days. The symptoms of CSF are clinically indistinguishable from those of African swine fever, making differential diagnosis essential. From an epidemiological perspective, CSF is endemic in many regions of Asia, Central and South America, as well as parts of Europe and Africa. The disease was declared eradicated in the United Kingdom in 1966, according to the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (DEFRA). However, an outbreak occurred in East Anglia in 2000. In the United States, CSF was eradicated by 1978, as reported by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Other regions considered free of CSF include Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, and Scandinavia. The causative agent of CSF is the Classical Swine Fever Virus (CSFV), which belongs to the genus Pestivirus within the family Flaviviridae (formerly classified under Togaviridae). CSFV is closely related to other pestiviruses, such as those responsible for Bovine Viral Diarrhea Virus (BVDV) and Border Disease Virus (BDV). The virulence of CSFV strains varies significantly, leading to a spectrum of clinical presentations. Highly virulent strains are associated with acute disease, severe neurological symptoms, hemorrhages in the skin, and high mortality rates. Conversely, less virulent strains may cause subacute or chronic infections, which can evade detection but still result in fetal or neonatal mortality. Infected piglets born to subclinically infected sows play a critical role in perpetuating the disease within a population. Additional symptoms of CSF include lethargy, fever, immunosuppression, and secondary respiratory infections. The incubation period for CSFV ranges from 2 to 14 days, but clinical signs may not manifest until 2 to 4 weeks post-infection. Animals with acute infections may survive for 2 to 3 months before succumbing to the disease. Eradication of CSF poses significant challenges. Potential sources of infection include the movement of pigs and pork products, as well as the presence of endemic CSF in wild boar and feral pig populations. Diagnosis of CSF involves a combination of epidemiological assessment, clinical symptomatology, pathological findings, and laboratory testing. Laboratory diagnostic methods include: Direct immunofluorescence: Used to detect the virus in histological tissue samples. Indirect immunofluorescence: Employed to identify specific antibodies in serum samples. Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA): Utilized for the detection of viral antigens or antibodies. A notable outbreak of hog cholera occurred in the Philippines in 2007. On August 20, 2007, the Department of Agriculture investigated a swine flu outbreak in Nueva Ecija and Central Luzon. Although the mortality rate for swine flu was reported to be less than 10% in the absence of complications such as hog cholera, the situation raised significant concerns. Earlier, on July 27, 2007, the Philippine National Meat Inspection Service (NMIS) issued a red alert for hog cholera in Metro Manila and five regions of Luzon. This alert followed the spread of the disease to backyard pig farms in Bulacan and Pampanga, despite these farms testing negative for the swine flu virus.
